sections.Challenge overview:
Develop a technology-enabled solution that can clear blocked culverts used for drainage without requiring human intervention at the blockage, enabling the drainage passage to be restored through a repeatable field process.
The Directorate of Town and Country Planning, Assam has submitted this challenge as a need for technology to clean blocked culverts for drainage without human intervention. The Directorate’s official website describes its role in planned urban development and notes that implementation of schemes includes Drainage Divisions at Guwahati and Tinsukia. The submission, however, does not specify the frequency or causes of blockage, the types and dimensions of culverts involved, the nature of the obstructions, or the current method used for cleaning.
The intended operational users are therefore the drainage/field teams and other authorised implementing agencies responsible for the affected drainage assets. The exact operating context is to be confirmed by the Directorate before publication.

sections.Challenge overview:
Improve the timeliness and spatial specificity of crop-health monitoring while adding stronger pest and disease forecasting so farmers and field teams can identify crop stress and emerging threats earlier and take targeted action.

Crop stress, pest and disease incidence, and nutrient deficiencies may not be identified early or uniformly through field-based observation alone. The Agriculture Department also reports that some pests and diseases can emerge suddenly and spread rapidly, causing large-scale crop damage, while farmers may find it difficult to manage new or sudden outbreaks.
Current operational context: ASSAC proposes repeated observation using satellite, UAV/drone and field information and conversion of those observations into actionable location-specific advisories. The Agriculture Department notes that forecasting models are currently available only for certain specific pests and diseases and that their full utility has not yet been achieved by farmers. It also identifies the need for deeper work on pest/disease epidemiology to support robust forecasting.
The intended users and operational stakeholders are farmers, agriculture/horticulture field staff, extension workers and district authorities.

For pest/disease forecasting, the Agriculture Department points to scientific epidemiology-based research and support from specialised startups. These are indicative directions; alternative evidence-based analytics and methods are welcome.

The solution should provide confidence levels, field-verification workflows, multilingual/mobile-friendly advisories where feasible, and an auditable record of observations and advisories.

sections.What a solution should enable:
A proposal does not need to follow a single technology path, but it should demonstrate how the following capabilities would be delivered in the stated government context:
• Develop a low-cost system that combines tamper-proof digital identity, batch-level traceability and rapid non-destructive authentication, delivered through a simple mobile app for field staff and consumers.
• Identity layer: Assign each cocoon lot a batch ID at the rearer or reeler level and link it to the yarn lot, fabric roll and garment. Garments should carry a tamper-evident QR or NFC tag stitched into the label.
• Record layer: Log each handover (rearer → reeler → weaver → retailer) with actor ID, date, quantity and GPS or cluster code. Hashes should be anchored on a permissioned blockchain so records cannot be edited afterwards; personal data should remain off-chain.

Candidate methods stated in the submission include handheld NIR or Raman spectroscopy, smartphone macro-imaging with an AI classifier for fibre structure and lustre, and hyperspectral imaging for lab-grade confirmation.
• App layer: Provide a lightweight Android app in Assamese and English. Field staff should be able to scan, log and test; consumers should be able to scan the tag to view origin, chain of custody and test status. The app should work offline and sync when connectivity returns.

sections.Challenge overview:
Upper Assam and Assam-Arakan crude is highly paraffinic, with pour points often at or above ambient winter temperatures. During colder months, wax crystallisation within gathering lines and trunk pipelines can cause the crude to gel and significantly increase restart pressures. Operators currently manage this through imported polymeric pour point depressants, line heating, hot-oil circulation and more frequent pigging. These measures involve recurring cost, energy consumption and shutdown risk, while imported additives may require higher dosages and show variable performance as crude characteristics change with field ageing and rising water cut.

The crude also reaches group gathering stations as a stable water-in-oil emulsion. Dehydration currently relies on heater-treaters operating at elevated temperatures together with conventional demulsifiers. This consumes station fuel gas and crude, contributes to emissions, and can still leave basic sediment and water levels near the upper end of the acceptable range during winter, occasionally resulting in rejection at the refinery gate.

The challenge affects field production operations, crude oil pipelines and transportation, and installation chemistry and laboratory functions. It is a chronic issue across gathering stations, group gathering stations and trunk pipeline segments in the region, recurring through every winter cycle and becoming more pronounced as fields mature.
The affected geography includes the Upper Assam districts of Tinsukia, Dibrugarh, Sivasagar, Charaideo and Jorhat, adjoining fields in Arunachal Pradesh, with potential extension to Tripura. The issue persists throughout the operating year but is most acute during November to February. Its operational impact includes recurring expenditure on additives, heating fuel, pigging and downtime, with the exact business impact to be quantified jointly with the nominated asset during pilot scoping. At present, no indigenous additive chemistry is available at commercial scale that is specifically formulated for the wax crystal morphology and interfacial chemistry of North-East crude.

Success would be reflected in reduced dependence on line heating and hot-oil circulation, lower additive dosage per tonne of crude, lower fuel-gas and energy consumption at gathering stations, and fewer flow-restriction or restart incidents during winter. The solution should be import-substituting, manufacturable in India, and supported by a laboratory screening protocol that enables reformulation as the crude slate changes.

Key desired outcomes are:
- Lower treated-crude pour point suitable for sub-4°C transport conditions.
- Lower additive dosage at equal or better performance.
- Significant reduction in crude dehydration temperature while maintaining the required BS&W specification.
- Measurable reduction in fuel-gas or energy consumption per tonne of crude treated.

sections.Challenge overview:
Pipelines carrying North-East waxy crude lose effective bore steadily as paraffin lays down on the inner wall. Operators cannot see this happening. Deposition is inferred indirectly from pressure drop trends and from what comes back on the pig, which means pigging is scheduled on a calendar basis rather than on condition. The result is both over-pigging, which costs production time and pigging effort on lines that did not need it, and under-pigging, which allows deposits to build to the point of restriction, stuck pigs or an unplanned shutdown. Chemical inhibitor dosing suffers from the same blindness and is set conservatively rather than to actual need.

Running in parallel is microbiologically influenced corrosion. Sulphate-reducing bacteria in produced water and in sludge under wax deposits drive rapid, localised pinhole failure. Present practice relies on periodic coupon retrieval and laboratory culture counts, which take days to return a result and sample only a few locations. By the time an elevated count is reported, the corrosion event is often already underway. Wax and bio-corrosion are physically linked — deposits shelter the bacterial colonies — yet they are monitored by entirely separate and entirely retrospective methods.

This affects pipeline operations, inspection and integrity management, and the corrosion and chemical treatment functions. It applies across the ageing crude gathering and trunk network of the region, much of which crosses high-rainfall terrain, agricultural land, wetlands and river crossings where the environmental consequence of a leak is disproportionate to its size.

sections.Challenge overview:
The North-East has a significant number of small and marginal gas discoveries and associated gas streams that remain beyond the reach of trunk pipeline infrastructure. At the volumes involved, conventional pipelines are often uneconomic, while difficult terrain, forest clearances and river crossings further increase development costs. As a result, gas may be flared, re-injected or left undeveloped, leading to loss of a saleable resource and avoidable emissions.
Existing alternatives remain limited. CNG cascade evacuation by road is constrained by low payload and deteriorating economics over distance, while conventional liquefaction systems are generally designed for volumes much larger than those produced by marginal fields and involve capital and footprint requirements that are difficult to justify at the wellhead. Micro gas-to-liquids and wellhead power generation exist internationally, but have not been demonstrated at Indian marginal-field scale in this terrain and at an approvable capital cost.

The challenge affects upstream field development and production, gas marketing, and regional industrial and commercial consumers. At the same time, industrial units, tea estates, brick kilns and commercial fleets across Assam and neighbouring states continue to depend on diesel, furnace oil and coal because clean gaseous fuel does not reach them. The issue therefore reflects both stranded gas supply and unmet regional demand existing within the same geography.

- Affected assets: Marginal and isolated gas fields and associated-gas points across the Assam-Arakan basin that lack pipeline connectivity.
- Affected stakeholders: Upstream asset and gas marketing teams, along with industrial, commercial and transport fuel consumers across the North-East.

sections.Challenge overview:
Plucking is the single most labour-intensive operation in tea cultivation and directly determines made-tea quality. The industry in Assam and Dooars faces large-scale and ever-increasing labour absenteeism and a rising shortage and cost of skilled manual pluckers. This makes it increasingly difficult to maintain a tight 7-day plucking round, which is essential for preserving leaf quality. Existing options such as battery-operated shears and one- or two-person harvesting machines reduce manpower but pluck indiscriminately, compromising quality.

There is a critical need for a low-cost, field-deployable selective plucking mechanism capable of AI-driven identification and plucking of only the desired two-leaves-and-a-bud, thereby maintaining quality while significantly reducing dependence on manual labour. The solution must be suited to the narrow rows, uneven terrain and dense canopy typical of Assam and Dooars plantations

The solution should strengthen transparency across the supply chain, enable verification of origin and authenticity, improve visibility of green-leaf sourcing and batch movement, and support regulatory and market requirements. sections.Important implementation consideration:
Interoperability rather than replacement: The proposed system should therefore be capable of exchanging data with existing platforms without requiring wholesale replacement of current infrastructure

Small-grower usability: The Assam ecosystem includes both large estates and numerous small tea growers. The solution should therefore be simple to adopt, cost-effective and usable by participants with differing levels of digital infrastructure.

Data ownership and confidentiality: Traceability requires sharing information across multiple actors, but not all commercial information should necessarily be visible to every participant. The architecture should support role-based access, appropriate permissions and protection of commercially sensitive information.

Data quality and standardisation: Different actors may currently record information in different formats or through manual processes. The solution should accommodate heterogeneous inputs while creating a sufficiently standardised traceability record.

Offline / low-connectivity environments: Field-level usage may occur in areas with inconsistent connectivity; proposed approaches should account for this wherever relevant.

Identity and chain-of-custody integrity: The usefulness of the platform will depend not merely on recording data, but on establishing confidence that the actor, batch and event being recorded correspond to the actual supply-chain transaction.

Blending and transformation: Tea does not necessarily remain as a single unchanged batch throughout the value chain. The architecture should be able to maintain traceability when batches are split, combined, blended, processed or repackaged.

Scalability and cost: The eventual system may need to support a large number of growers, factories, batches and transactions. Architecture and operating costs should therefore be suitable for deployment beyond the pilot.

Regulatory alignment: The solution should be capable of accommodating applicable Tea Board, food-safety, testing, data-protection and other relevant requirements without hard-coding itself to a single current workflow.

sections.Challenge overview:
This fragmentation makes it difficult to obtain timely, standardized, and reliable information on what is being collected, where it is located or moving, how much is recovered or processed, and where operational bottlenecks exist. Precise geolocation of waste generation, collection points, accumulated waste and operational activities is not consistently available, limiting location-based monitoring and response.

The challenge is particularly significant in Guwahati, where approximately 550 tonnes of solid waste are managed daily across 31 wards, involving multiple collection agencies and frontline workers. GMC also operates secondary collection and transportation infrastructure, including transfer stations.

Current monitoring relies significantly on information independently collected and reported by different stakeholders. The absence of a common digital platform can result in information silos, delayed reporting, inconsistent data, and limited end-to-end visibility.

This impacts ULBs, waste-management operators, frontline workers, MRFs, processing facilities, recyclers, and other ecosystem stakeholders, limiting their ability to identify missed collections, waste accumulation hotspots, transportation inefficiencies, recovery opportunities, processing constraints and material movement.

The key requirement is a centralized digital waste-management platform that connects stakeholders and operational stages through a common intelligent data layer, incorporating geolocation and near-real-time field data. The platform should provide a single source of operational transparency, while remaining practical for frontline use and scalable from Guwahati to other Urban/ Rural Local Bodies across Assam.

It should support low-bandwidth and offline operation, minimise manual data entry through automation, and provide simple, intuitive interfaces for different user types. The solution should also incorporate appropriate access controls for personal and operational data, avoid unnecessary dependence on expensive end-user hardware, support relevant local-language requirements where needed, and enable interoperability with existing government or ULB systems where feasible. sections.What a solution should enable:
The solution should enable authorised stakeholders to move from fragmented, periodic reporting to a single, continuously updated operational view, with reliable geospatial and activity-level data that can support day-to-day management and emergency response.

Specifically, the solution should achieve:
•	≥90% coverage of agreed pilot collection, transportation, recovery and processing activities, with standardized digital records.
•	Near-real-time capture and availability of key operational data, with agreed priority data points visible to authorised users within 24 hours or less.
•	≥90% geospatial accuracy/coverage for agreed waste collection points, reported accumulation hotspots, facilities and field activities, enabling location-based monitoring.
•	End-to-end traceability for agreed waste streams, allowing users to track quantities collected, transported, recovered, processed, rejected and, where feasible, their destination.
•	Integrated visibility across stakeholders, consolidating data from participating agencies, operators, facilities and frontline teams into a common operational view.
•	Faster identification and response to operational gaps, including missed collection, waste accumulation, route inefficiencies, facility capacity constraints and abnormal material flows.
•	Emergency waste-management visibility, enabling authorities to identify, geotag and monitor waste accumulation and collection requirements during floods and other periods of disruption.
•	Actionable dashboards, alerts and reports that enable ULBs and authorised stakeholders to identify trends, allocate resources and make evidence-based operational decisions.
•	High frontline usability, with at least 80% of participating frontline users actively contributing data without significant additional reporting burden.
•	Scalability, with the solution capable of extending from the initial Guwahati pilot to additional ULBs and districts across Assam.

summary: The challenge seeks a centralized digital waste-management platform that connects collection, transportation, recovery, processing, recycling and disposal through a common data layer with geolocation and near-real-time field information.
